newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British open Hong Kong consulate as handover nears.
newsitem.headline: British open Hong Kong consulate as handover nears.

text.p: To the drumbeat of a traditional Chinese lion dance, the British formally opened a consulate in Hong Kong on Thursday, another step on the way to the end of more than 150 years of colonial rule.
Princess Anne made what will probably be her last visit to Hong Kong as a British colony to open the building, perched on the brow of a low hill near the territory's Supreme Court.
When the red flag of China flutters over Hong Kong on July 1, the official British presence will be contained in the consulate, just one of dozens of consulates in Hong Kong.
It has been more than a decade since Britain and China sealed Hong Kong's fate in the 1984 Joint Declaration.

That treaty bound the British to cede sovereignty of their last Asian outpost at midnight on June 30, 1997, and requires China to maintain Hong Kong's capitalist freedoms and way of life intact for 50 years.
The intervening years have been bumpy ones with the two sovereign states at loggerheads much of the time, particularly over democratic reforms introduced in the final years of British rule.
The gulf shows no signs of narrowing as the clock ticks down to the handover, now just 152 days away.
China's proposals to dilute Hong Kong's laws guaranteeing civil liberties, including a Bill of Rights, has sparked outrage in the British colony and forceful objections from London and its allies.

The British minister with responsibility for Hong Kong said upon arriving for a brief visit on Wednesday that Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind would make British views clear at a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen next month.

Members of China's handpicked Preparatory Committee were preparing for a meeting in Beijing on Friday and Saturday to determine the fate of the 25 laws and articles, some the product of recent reforms, others the trappings of the colonial era, that Beijing proposes repealing or amending.
The 150-member committee of mainland officials and Hong Kong worthies was set up last year to transform Hong Kong from a British colony into a Special Administrative Region of China.
China argues the ordinances clash with the Basic Law, the constitution Beijing promulgated for post-1997 Hong Kong, but insists basic freedoms in the territory would not be affected.
U.S. President Bill Clinton weighed in on Wednesday urging China to refrain from crushing civil liberties in Hong Kong.

"I'm not so sure that it can exist with all of its potential to help China modernise its own economy and open opportunities for its own people, if the civil liberties of the people are crushed," Clinton told a news conference.
"So I think it would be wrong on its own merits, but I think it might wind up being less useful to China."
Anne toured Hong Kong on Thursday.
Half a century ago her great uncle, Lord Mountbatten, presided over independence for India -- the beginning of the end of the British empire.
Exactly 50 years later, Anne's brother and heir to the British throne, Prince Charles, will sail into Hong Kong to preside when Britain gives up the last important possession of its empire.
